evidence.label: Global Support and Convex Injectivity Domains under Weak MTW
Uniform Bi-Holder Transport from Weak MTW

headline: Proves weak MTW curvature makes every injectivity domain convex, as Villani conjectured, and transport maps Hölder.
scope: Compact connected boundaryless Riemannian manifolds of dimension at least two satisfying the weak Ma–Trudinger–Wang condition, with transport between densities bounded above and below.
plain: Optimal transport asks for the cheapest way to move one spread of mass to another, with cost equal to half the squared distance. On a curved space, a curvature condition called weak MTW controls this cost where it is smooth. The first paper proves that this condition makes every injectivity domain convex, as Villani conjectured. The second proves that the best transport map and its inverse are Hölder continuous, with one constant for a whole class of densities. Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal statements of both main results.
doesNot: This does not give an explicit Hölder exponent, or constants that stay uniform when the metric changes. The Lean scope also omits the paper's arbitrary-potential local-injectivity assertion.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Xi-Nan Ma, Neil Trudinger and Xu-Jia Wang, a curvature condition for optimal transport regularity
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles Villani's conjecture without nonfocality and gives class-uniform transport regularity, both with Lean statements.

explanation:
Take a flat square torus of side 1, like a video-game screen where leaving one edge brings you back on the opposite edge. Stand at a point x and walk straight with velocity v. If v = (0.4, 0.3), you travel length 0.5 and no shorter path exists. If v = (0.6, 0), you end 0.4 away on the other side, so your straight path was not the shortest. The velocities whose straight paths stay shortest a little beyond time one form an open set called the injectivity domain[2]. On this torus it is the open square where both coordinates lie strictly between −1/2 and 1/2. That square is convex: the midpoint of (0.45, 0.1) and (0.1, 0.45) is (0.275, 0.275), still inside.

Optimal transport moves one spread of mass to another at least total cost. Here the cost of moving from x to y is half the squared distance. The Ma–Trudinger–Wang condition, MTW for short, is a curvature condition on this cost. The weak version only asks for a sign in directions perpendicular to each other[3]. Villani proposed that weak MTW forces every injectivity domain to be convex[4]. Figalli, Gallouët and Rifford proved this for nonfocal manifolds, where shortest paths stop being shortest before nearby paths refocus[5]. The obstacle is that the cost stops being smooth along some proposed paths. Weak MTW controls only directions perpendicular to the path[6].

The first paper proves the conjecture on every compact connected manifold of dimension at least two without boundary[1]. Points where nearby paths refocus are allowed[7]. It also shows that every ordinary subgradient of a cost potential is a shortest velocity with a global supporting mountain[8]. No assumption on densities is used.

The second paper uses this to control the transport map. Fix densities with upper bound Λ and positive lower bound λ. The best map T and its inverse then obey d(T(x), T(x′)) ≤ C d(x, x′)^α[9]. This is Hölder continuity. For example, with α = 1/2, points 0.01 apart go to points at most 0.1 C apart. The constants α and C work for the whole class of densities on a fixed manifold[10]. The exponent is found by contradiction, so no explicit value is given[11]. With an earlier result of Figalli, Rifford and Villani, this gives an equivalence between weak MTW and continuity of transport[12].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal statements of both main results. So the papers prove them, as far as the Lean statements match the papers. One local-injectivity statement is covered only for finite target families. No specialist review is published.
hypeCheck: Major, with Lean statements of both main results. The Hölder exponent is not explicit, and the constants depend on the fixed manifold. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: Moving one spread of mass to another at the least total cost.
The set of starting velocities whose straight paths stay shortest a little beyond time one.
A sign condition on a fourth derivative of the squared-distance cost, asked only in perpendicular directions.
Containing the whole straight segment between any two of its points.
A manifold where shortest paths stop being shortest strictly before nearby paths refocus.
Moving close points to close points, with distance controlled by a power of the original distance.
A slope that supports a function from below at a point, even where it has a corner.
